title: Coordinate Geometry
summary: Chapter 7 of NCERT Class 10 Mathematics covers Coordinate Geometry, which explores the relationship between geometry and algebra through the Cartesian coordinate system. The chapter explains distance formula, section formula, area of triangles, and conditions for collinearity of points. It establishes how to plot points on a plane and use algebraic methods to solve geometric problems. The chapter also covers the concept of slope of a line, various forms of linear equations, and conditions for parallelism and perpendicularity of lines. Coordinate Geometry provides powerful tools for solving complex geometric problems using algebraic techniques and forms the foundation for advanced studies in mathematics.

sections.heading: Cartesian Coordinate System
sections.para: The Cartesian coordinate system consists of two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, intersecting at origin O. Any point P in the plane is represented by ordered pair (x,y) where x is the distance from y-axis and y is the distance from x-axis. The coordinate axes divide the plane into four quadrants. In first quadrant, both x and y are positive; in second quadrant, x is negative and y is positive; in third quadrant, both are negative; and in fourth quadrant, x is positive and y is negative. The distance of a point from origin is given by sqrt(x^2 + y^2).

sections.heading: Distance Formula
sections.para: The distance between two points P(x1,y1) and Q(x2,y2) in a plane is given by the formula PQ = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). This formula is derived from Pythagoras theorem by considering the horizontal and vertical distances between the points. The distance is always positive. When finding distance between points, it doesn't matter which point is taken as first or second. For points on the x-axis, y1=y2=0, so distance is |x2-x1|. For points on the y-axis, x1=x2=0, so distance is |y2-y1|. The distance formula is fundamental in coordinate geometry and used to solve many problems.

sections.heading: Section Formula
sections.para: The section formula divides a line segment joining two points P(x1,y1) and Q(x2,y2) in a given ratio m:n. The coordinates of the point R dividing PQ internally in ratio m:n are ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n)). For external division, the coordinates are ((mx2-nx1)/(m-n), (my2-ny1)/(m-n)). When m:n = 1:1, the formula gives midpoint coordinates ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2). The section formula is used to find centroid of triangle, which divides each median in 2:1 ratio. The formula is also used to find points dividing a line segment in given ratio for various geometric constructions.

sections.heading: Area of Triangle
sections.para: The area of triangle with vertices A(x1,y1), B(x2,y2), and C(x3,y3) can be calculated using the formula: Area = 1/2 |x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)|. The absolute value ensures the area is always positive. If the area is zero, the points are collinear. This formula is derived from the concept of determinants and provides a quick method to find area without drawing the triangle. The formula can be extended to find area of polygons by dividing them into triangles. For a right-angled triangle with legs parallel to axes, the area simplifies to 1/2 × base × height where base and height are the differences in x and y coordinates respectively.

sections.heading: Collinearity of Points
sections.para: Three points are collinear if they lie on the same straight line. There are three main methods to check collinearity: area method, slope method, and distance method. Using area method, if the area of triangle formed by three points is zero, the points are collinear. Using slope method, if the slope of line joining first two points equals slope of line joining second and third points, the points are collinear. Using distance method, if the sum of distances between two pairs of points equals the distance between the third pair, the points are collinear. The area method is most commonly used as it involves direct calculation without finding slopes or distances.

sections.heading: Slope of a Line
sections.para: The slope of a line is a measure of its steepness and direction. For a line passing through points P(x1,y1) and Q(x2,y2), the slope m is given by m = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1). The slope is undefined for vertical lines (where x1=x2) and zero for horizontal lines (where y1=y2). Positive slope indicates the line rises from left to right, while negative slope indicates it falls from left to right. The slope is also equal to tanθ where θ is the angle the line makes with the positive x-axis. Slope is fundamental in determining the nature of lines and their relationships.

sections.heading: Equations of Lines
sections.para: A straight line can be represented by various forms of equations. The slope-intercept form is y = mx + c where m is slope and c is y-intercept. The point-slope form is y - y1 = m(x - x1) where (x1,y1) is a point on the line. The two-point form is (y-y1)/(y2-y1) = (x-x1)/(x2-x1) where (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) are two points. The intercept form is x/a + y/b = 1 where a and b are x and y intercepts. The general form is Ax + By + C = 0 where A, B, C are constants. These forms can be converted into each other using algebraic manipulations. Each form is useful for different types of problems involving lines.

sections.heading: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
sections.para: Two lines are parallel if their slopes are equal. If line 1 has slope m1 and line 2 has slope m2, then m1 = m2 for parallel lines. Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their slopes is -1, i.e., m1 × m2 = -1. A horizontal line has slope 0 and is parallel to all other horizontal lines. A vertical line has undefined slope and is parallel to all other vertical lines. A horizontal line is perpendicular to all vertical lines. These conditions are used to find equations of lines parallel or perpendicular to given lines, and to determine the relationship between lines in geometric problems.

sections.heading: Applications of Coordinate Geometry
sections.para: Coordinate Geometry has numerous applications in solving geometric problems. It is used to find distances between points, divide line segments in given ratios, calculate areas of triangles and polygons, verify collinearity, find equations of lines, and determine relationships between lines. It is also used to solve real-world problems involving positions, paths, and areas. In higher mathematics, coordinate geometry forms the basis for analytical geometry, calculus, and other advanced topics. The concepts learned in this chapter are essential for understanding more complex geometric and algebraic relationships.

mcqs.question: If a and b are two positive integers such that a = 6b and b = 48, then what is the HCF of a and b?
mcqs.explanation: Since a = 6b and b = 48, a = 6 × 48 = 288. The HCF of 288 and 48 is 24, as 24 is the largest number that divides both.

mcqs.explanation: For a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c, sum of zeroes = -b/a. Here, a = 1, b = -5, so alpha + beta = 5.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that sqrt(3) is irrational.
boardQuestions.answer: Let's assume sqrt(3) is rational. Then sqrt(3) = p/q, where p and q are coprime integers. Squaring both sides, 3 = p^2/q^2, so p^2 = 3q^2. This means p^2 is divisible by 3, so p is divisible by 3 (since 3 is prime). Let p = 3k. Then (3k)^2 = 3q^2, so 9k^2 = 3q^2, thus q^2 = 3k^2. This means q^2 is divisible by 3, so q is divisible by 3. But if both p and q are divisible by 3, they are not coprime, which contradicts our assumption. Therefore, sqrt(3) must be irrational.

boardQuestions.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18 using prime factorisation.
boardQuestions.answer: Prime factorisation of 12 = 2^2 × 3. Prime factorisation of 18 = 2 × 3^2. HCF is the product of the lowest powers of common prime factors: 2^1 × 3^1 = 6. LCM is the product of the highest powers of all prime factors: 2^2 × 3^2 = 36. Therefore, HCF = 6 and LCM = 36.

boardQuestions.question: Find the zeroes of the polynomial x^2 - 5x + 6 and verify the relationship between zeroes and coefficients.
boardQuestions.answer: To find zeroes, solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0. Factorizing, (x-2)(x-3) = 0, so zeroes are 2 and 3. For a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c, sum of zeroes = -b/a and product = c/a. Here, a = 1, b = -5, c = 6. Sum of zeroes = 2 + 3 = 5, which equals -(-5)/1 = 5. Product of zeroes = 2 × 3 = 6, which equals 6/1 = 6. The relationship is verified.

boardQuestions.question: Solve the pair of linear equations: 2x + 3y = 7 and 4x - y = 11.
boardQuestions.answer: Multiply the first equation by 2: 4x + 6y = 14. Subtract the second equation: (4x + 6y) - (4x - y) = 14 - 11, so 7y = 3, thus y = 3/7. Substitute into second equation: 4x - (3/7) = 11, so 4x = 11 + 3/7 = 80/7, thus x = 20/7. The solution is x = 20/7, y = 3/7.

boardQuestions.question: Find the discriminant and nature of roots of the quadratic equation 3x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0.
boardQuestions.answer: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0, discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac. Here, a = 3, b = -5, c = 2. D = (-5)^2 - 4(3)(2) = 25 - 24 = 1. Since D > 0 and is a perfect square, the roots are real, rational, and unequal.

boardQuestions.question: Find the 15th term of the AP: 3, 8, 13, 18, ...
boardQuestions.answer: First term a = 3, common difference d = 8 - 3 = 5. nth term of AP = a + (n-1)d. For n = 15, 15th term = 3 + (15-1)(5) = 3 + 14(5) = 3 + 70 = 73.

boardQuestions.question: In triangle ABC, angle B = 90°, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm. Find AC and verify Pythagoras theorem.
boardQuestions.answer: By Pythagoras theorem, AC = sqrt(AB^2 + BC^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 cm. To verify, check if AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2: 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100, and 10^2 = 100. Since both sides equal 100, Pythagoras theorem is verified.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
boardQuestions.answer: Consider triangle ABC with a line DE parallel to BC intersecting AB at D and AC at E. Draw perpendiculars from D and E to BC, meeting at P and Q. Since DE || BC, triangles ADE and ABC are similar by AA criterion (angle A is common, and angle ADE = angle ABC). Therefore, AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC. Also, since DE || BC, triangles DBP and ECQ are similar. Thus, AD/DB = AE/EC. Hence, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.

boardQuestions.question: Find the coordinates of the point which divides the line segment joining (1, 2) and (3, 4) in the ratio 2:1.
boardQuestions.answer: Using section formula, coordinates = ((mx2 + nx1)/(m+n), (my2 + ny1)/(m+n)), where m:n = 2:1. So, x = (2×3 + 1×1)/(2+1) = (6+1)/3 = 7/3. y = (2×4 + 1×2)/(2+1) = (8+2)/3 = 10/3. The coordinates are (7/3, 10/3).

boardQuestions.question: If sin A = 3/5, find cos A and tan A.
boardQuestions.answer: Using sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1, (3/5)^2 + cos^2 A = 1, so 9/25 + cos^2 A = 1, thus cos^2 A = 16/25, so cos A = 4/5 (acute angle). tan A = sin A/cos A = (3/5)/(4/5) = 3/4.
